video.titulo: California's Most Dangerous Fault Isn't Overdue — USGS Said Something Worse
video.descricao:
Sources: https://tinyurl.com/critical26
Emergency Preparedness Guide: https://payhip.com/b/GWENV

The Hayward Fault is not overdue. That word never came from the U.S. Geological Survey, and the numbers underneath it say something a good deal more uncomfortable.

Here is what is actually happening. The fault runs under more than 300 buildings and structures, straight under the University of California Berkeley football stadium, and it is bending a curb in the city of Hayward by about a fifth of an inch — five millimeters — every year. The USGS HayWired scenario, a magnitude 7.0 starting beneath Oakland, projects 800 deaths, roughly 18,000 injuries, more than $82 billion in damage, over 400 separate fires, and East Bay neighborhoods without water for six weeks.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The Hayward Fault Is Bending a Curb Right Now
2:16 What the 1868 Earthquake Actually Did
3:27 Why a Creeping Fault Is Not Good News
5:02 HayWired: 800 Deaths and Six Weeks Without Water
7:07 The Supercomputer Result Nobody Expected
8:26 How We Know What Happened in the Year 1134
9:41 The USGS Number Everyone Misquotes
11:48 "Expected at Any Time" — Their Words, Not Mine
13:45 The Pipe Built to Survive It

Have you ever felt an earthquake? Where were you, and what was the first thing you did? Tell me in the comments.

Subscribe to Critical Latitude for more on earthquakes, faults, volcanoes and what the planet is doing, with the real science behind it. The next video is about the six weeks of water.

SOURCES AND DISCLAIMER
Everything here comes off three documents: two U.S. Geological Survey fact sheets — one written by six of their earthquake geologists about this specific fault, one from the team behind the HayWired scenario — and a paper in Geophysical Research Letters from a group at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory who modeled the shaking on a supercomputer.

Was at work at Stanford, in a modern 5-story building for 6.9 1989 quake.  Much of the damage was not external, but some buildings were red-tagged for repair and seismic reinforcement.  Initially, Stanford estimated >$200 million damage (1989 dollars) but pre-quake plans for a new quad were shelved for nearly a decade.  Was in Mountain View, in 2nd-floor apartment, working on computer at 3:30am, when radio news announced the 6.0 2014 Napa EQ, but didn't feel anything.  California's much contorted tectonic terrane is known to attenuate/dampen seismic energy more quickly than in the eastern US, where basement bedrock is much older and more solid.  Per USGS, a 6.0 quake in California might be felt across 6 adjacent counties, maybe.  A 6.0 quake in Kentucky might be felt in a dozen, or more, adjacent states, at least!  Terrane like the Appalachians predates the last supercontinent phase.  The San Andreas Fault Zone has only existed about 30 million or less years, and California's hilly and mountainous landscape is strewn with younger, mixed, sedimentary deposits, which can amplify shallow seismic energy while attenuating deeper seismic waves.

I do have one complaint however: at 8:53 you claim that "nobody wrote those [events] down; there was nobody there to write them down".  That claim isn't exactly true.   There were tens (if not, hundreds) of thousands of Native Americans living in the Bay Area prior to European contact; specifically Miwok and Ohlone. These people most certainly kept an ORAL record of earthquakes. For example, Makkeweks was a subterranean spirit that was associated with earthquakes, flooding, and tsunamis (there's actually a statue at Snow Park in Oakland); evidence that points to common knowledge of earthquakes among the Native people in the region.  The Spanish missionaries that arrived in the 1770’s began to put a stop to Native oral traditions and religious practices. After European arrival, and especially during the Gold Rush, California was the location of the greatest Native American genocide; and it gets largely ignored. Spanish missionaries did record seismic events and some of the native knowledge, but only in terms that benefitted their points of view, belief system, and record keeping system. So their records carry the same dubious reliability that oral record keeping is supposed to have.   When you also consider the rampant development of the Bay Area since the 1770's, it's no surprise that any record that could have survived, has since been lost.  To be clear, I'm not trying to roast you or imply that you're a terrible person. You just said something that was incorrect, and I hoped to set the "record" straight (pun intended).
